subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Substitution: Answering an Easier Question
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Substitution: Answering an Easier Question.

hook.text: Asked 'how happy are you with life?' people answer about today's mood. They've swapped the question.

buildup.text: Kahneman calls this attribute substitution. When a question is hard, we answer a similar easier one.

discovery.text: We rarely notice the swap. The easy answer feels like it fits the hard question perfectly.

twist.text: 'Is this CEO competent?' becomes 'does this CEO look confident?' Appearance answers for ability.

climax.text: Catch the substitution by restating the original question. 'Wait, what was I actually asked?'

punchline.text: If the answer came too fast, check the question.

quiz.question: What is attribute substitution?
options: Answering a hard question by replacing it with an easier one

details.summary: Attribute substitution occurs when faced with a difficult question and people unknowingly answer an easier, related question instead. Asked how satisfied they are with life, they answer how they feel right now. Asked about probability, they answer about vividness.
details.whyItMatters: Substitution is the core mechanism behind many cognitive biases. People believe they are answering the actual question when they are answering a simpler proxy.
takeaways: Difficult questions are unconsciously replaced with easier substitute questions
People are unaware the substitution has occurred and believe they answered the original
Most cognitive biases can be traced to specific attribute substitutions

faq.question: What is a common example of attribute substitution?
faq.answer: The question 'How likely is this investment to succeed?' is difficult and requires research. The easier substitute is 'How do I feel about this investment?' The answer to the feeling question is used as the answer to the probability question without awareness of the switch.

faq.question: Is attribute substitution always a mistake?
faq.answer: Not always. When the substitute attribute is well-correlated with the target attribute, substitution produces good enough answers quickly. The problem arises when the two attributes diverge, which happens systematically in cases like risk assessment and probability estimation.
